newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Klima says hopes for Creditanstalt offer.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Klima says hopes for Creditanstalt offer.

text.p: Austrian Finance Minister Viktor Klima said on Wednesday he still expected a firm offer for government sell-off candidate Creditanstalt to land on his desk before the end of the month.

A consortium of bidders led by savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische Spar-Casse Bank AG and insurer EA-Generali AG says it plans to set up a joint holding company for Creditanstalt, but has yet to present a final proposal.
"They have time until the end of August. I am available for a meeting at any time," Klima told journalists during an economic conference in the Tyrolean mountain resort of Alpbach.

He declined to speculate on whether the consortium, the only known bidder for the state's 70 percent stake in Austria's number two bank, would receive an extension if it failed to present its plans by Friday, the deadline he imposed last month.
But he said: "I expect that I will get an answer."

Under the plan, widely reported in Austrian media but never officially confirmed, Die Erste would hold one third of the holding company, EA-Generali and a host of other companies another third and small investors the remaining shares.
Klima hinted that the so-called "Austrian solution" was not the only possibility for the privatisation of Creditanstalt, which has been on the government's sell-off list for more than six years.
"There are still interested parties left from last year's negotiations. We wouldn't have to begin from scratch, only to go back one step," he said, without giving further details.

Several international bidders, including Germany's Allianz AG and CS Holding of Switzerland, have dropped out of the race for Creditanstalt in past years because of what they saw as a bias against foreign ownership in Austria's leading political circles.
Sources within Die Erste indicated that the group might be able to present a strategy paper before the end of the week. It was not immediately clear whether this would satisfy Klima's requirements.
Herbert Schimetschek, the savings bank's supervisory board president, said he could imagine a solution being found in September.
"I assume an offer will be put together. After all there are reasonable people on both sides," Austrian news agency APA quoted him as saying.
A study by investment house JP Morgan last year valued the government's stake at about 18 billion schillings ($1.7 billion).
